pages.text: The Student Council Election

image.note: Cover: campaign posters, a ballot box, two candidates

pages.text: Contents. Two Candidates / The Campaign / The Video / The Choice / The Debate / The Result.

"You could win this in a second," said Hanni, dropping onto the bench beside Amina and lowering her voice. "I found something. About Wali. Something that would finish him." She held up her phone, thumb hovering over a video. "One tap, and you send it to the whole class, and the election is yours." Amina looked at the phone. This was a moment she would remember for years.

image.note: Hanni offering the phone, Amina hesitating

pages.text: The estate school was choosing a new head of the student council, and for the first time the pupils themselves would vote. Two names went up on the board. Amina, who was eleven and organised and fair, and Wali, who was funny and popular and quick. Two good candidates, one job, and a whole school to win over.

image.note: The election board with two names

pages.text: Amina wanted it badly, and not for herself. She had real ideas: a proper football rota so the little ones got a turn, a lost-and-found box, a suggestion tin anyone could use. She had written them all out, neat and numbered, and she meant to win by being better, not louder.

image.note: Amina with her numbered list of ideas

pages.text: Her friend Hanni ran the campaign, and Hanni wanted to win at any cost. She made bright posters, chanted slogans, and watched Wali like a hawk for any slip. "He's beating us on jokes," Hanni fretted. "People vote for who makes them laugh. We need something big." Amina only shrugged. "We have the best ideas. Let the ideas win."

image.note: Hanni putting up posters, fretting

pages.text: For a week the school buzzed with it. Posters everywhere. Promises traded in the playground. Wali had the crowd laughing; Amina had the older ones nodding at her plans. It was close, everyone said, too close to call, and it would come down to the great debate on Friday, in front of the whole school.

image.note: A playground full of campaign posters

pages.text: Amina practised her points until she knew them cold. Hanni practised something else: digging. "Know your rival," she kept saying, scrolling and asking and listening. Amina did not like it much, but she was busy with her rota and her lost-and-found, and she did not ask what Hanni was digging for. She should have.

image.note: Amina rehearsing, Hanni scrolling on her phone

pages.text: On Thursday, Hanni found it. An old video, years old, from when Wali was small: a birthday party, a little boy who had eaten too much cake being loudly sick all down himself, in front of everyone, and crying. It was the kind of thing that follows a person around a school for ever, if the wrong people see it.

image.note: Hanni watching a video, eyes wide

pages.text: "This is it," Hanni whispered, finding Amina on the bench. "One tap. Send it to the class group. By tomorrow nobody will remember Wali's jokes. They will only remember this. He cannot beat that, Amina. Nobody could. The election is yours." And she held out the phone, the video ready, her thumb waiting.

image.note: Hanni holding out the phone, the video paused

pages.text: Amina looked at the phone for a long time. She thought about winning, which she wanted so much. Then she thought about Wali, small and sick and crying at his own party, and how it would feel to be that boy, laughed at by the whole school, for something he could not help, from years ago. Her stomach turned, and it was not the video.

image.note: Amina staring at the phone, torn

pages.text: "No," she said, and pushed the phone gently away. Hanni stared. "No? Amina, this wins it." "Then I don't want to win it," said Amina. "Not like that. If I have to shame a boy over being sick at a party when he was six, then I am not fit to lead anyone. Delete it, Hanni. And do not show a single soul."

image.note: Amina pushing the phone away, firm

pages.text: Hanni opened her mouth to argue, then closed it. Slowly she looked at the phone, at Amina's steady face, and something in her shifted. "You could lose," she said quietly. "I know," said Amina. "Delete it anyway." And after a long moment, Hanni did. Neither of them ever spoke of it again, but Hanni never forgot it either.

image.note: Hanni deleting the video, a changed look

pages.text: Friday came, and the whole school packed into the hall for the debate, Mrs Obi keeping order at the front. Wali went first, and had them laughing in a minute, easy and bright. Then Amina stood, her numbered list in her hand, her heart thumping, knowing she had no jokes, and no secret weapon, and nothing at all but her ideas.

image.note: The school hall, Amina standing to speak

pages.text: So she gave them her ideas. The football rota, so the small ones got their turn. The lost-and-found box. The suggestion tin, where any pupil, even the shyest, could ask for something to change. She spoke plainly and truly, and as she spoke, the laughing died down, and the hall grew quiet, and began, row by row, to listen.

image.note: The hall listening intently to Amina

pages.text: There was one moment, near the end, when Wali stumbled over an answer and went hot, and Hanni, in the front row, caught Amina's eye, one eyebrow raised: now, if you want him, now. Amina gave the smallest shake of her head, and moved on, and helped the moment pass, and let Wali find his feet again. Only three people in the hall knew what had just not happened.

image.note: Amina and Hanni exchanging a look, Wali recovering

pages.text: They voted on slips of paper, folded and dropped in a box, and Mrs Obi counted them twice to be sure, for it was close, terribly close. The whole school held its breath. Then she looked up, and smiled, and read the name. "Your new head of council," she said, "is Amina."

image.note: Mrs Obi reading the result, the school waiting

pages.text: The hall cheered, and Amina's ideas had won her the day, fair and square, with nothing hidden and nothing shamed. But the moment she remembered longest came after, when the crowd thinned, and Wali crossed the room to her, and put out his hand. "Good ideas," he said. "Better than my jokes. You won it right."

image.note: Wali shaking Amina's hand, both smiling

pages.text: "You were close," said Amina honestly. "You would have been good at it too." And she meant it. She never told him how close he had come to losing everything, not to her ideas, but to an old, cruel video that never saw the light. Some victories, she was learning, are the ones nobody ever sees.

image.note: Amina and Wali talking easily, the contest over

pages.text: Later, Hanni found her. "I still think we could have won faster," she said, but she was half smiling. "We won better," said Amina. "Faster is easy. Better is the whole point." And Hanni, who had learned something on that bench she would carry a long way, did not argue.

image.note: Amina and Hanni walking off together, friends

pages.text: Amina was head of the council for a year, and a good one. The football rota worked. The lost-and-found filled and emptied. The suggestion tin taught her a hundred things. But the best thing she ever did as a leader, she did before she was even elected, on a bench, with a phone held out, when she said one small, hard word: no.

image.note: Amina running a council meeting, the suggestion tin on the table

pages.text: The Election. Amina, who won with ideas, not dirt. Hanni, who learned the difference between faster and better. Wali, a good loser and a good sport. A reminder: how you win matters as much as whether you win, and the hardest, finest choices are often the ones nobody sees you make.

image.note: Amina, Hanni, and Wali together after the election
